title: Example Brief: General Writing Task
body:
# Example Brief: ML Recommendation Systems Article

This is a worked example of a completed, validated project brief. All fields are filled with realistic values. Use this as a reference when producing or evaluating briefs.

---

## Goal

Enable a technically literate but non-specialist reader to evaluate whether ML-based recommendation systems are appropriate for their product context, understand the key architectural tradeoffs, and identify the correct follow-up questions to ask their engineering team.

## Audience

Product managers and technical leads at mid-stage software companies (Series A–C). They have experience with software product development and can read pseudocode. They are not machine learning practitioners and have not built recommendation systems before. They are motivated by product outcomes (conversion, retention, engagement) rather than algorithmic elegance. They are skeptical of AI hype and will dismiss anything that sounds like vendor marketing. They read articles to make decisions, not to be educated for its own sake.

## Domain

general

## Tone

Semi-formal, authoritative, direct. No hedging. No corporate filler. Write as a knowledgeable practitioner who respects the reader's intelligence but does not assume their technical depth. Third-person perspective. No first person. Short paragraphs — maximum four sentences. Headers for every major section.

## Scope — In Scope

- How collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and hybrid approaches work at a conceptual level
- When each approach is appropriate given data availability, product maturity, and engineering capacity
- Key failure modes: the cold start problem, popularity bias, filter bubbles
- Rough infrastructure requirements and team skill requirements for each approach
- How to evaluate recommendation quality (offline metrics vs. online metrics)

## Scope — Out of Scope

- Deep mathematical treatment of matrix factorization or embedding models
- Specific vendor or open-source library comparisons
- Real-time vs. batch inference tradeoffs (flagged for a follow-up article)
- Personalization approaches that are not recommendation-system-based (e.g., A/B testing, segmentation)

## Constraints

- Target word count: 1,200–1,400 words
- No footnotes or citations (this is an explanatory article, not research)
- No tables wider than three columns
- Plain markdown output
- No jargon terms used without a brief inline definition on first use

## Deliverables

- One markdown article titled: "When to Use Machine Learning Recommendations (And When Not To)"
- Target: 1,200 words, 5–6 sections, no appendix
- Artifact format: markdown (.md)

## Success Criteria

- A product manager with no ML background can read the article and correctly answer: Which of the three approaches described is most appropriate for a new product with fewer than 1,000 active users?
- The skeptic QA perspective issues no BLOCK-level findings
- The reader QA perspective issues ACCEPT or CONDITIONAL_ACCEPT
- No AI-stink findings of severity HIGH from the qa-ai-stink agent

## Known Inputs

- No prior drafts exist
- No specific research report exists — section-drafter should rely on generally established knowledge
- Style pack: baseline-general (no domain-specific pack required)
- Example to follow: G-EXMP-002 (outline example based on this brief)
